LoLoRA achieves this by employing gradient-free updates to the A matrix, based on the layer's input, while simultaneously updating the B matrix using standard gradient-based optimization. This approach allows the model to adapt to input distribution shifts without the need to store activations for the backward pass, thereby reducing memory requirements. The authors provide a theoretical foundation for their method, demonstrating that the optimal initialization of the A matrix involves an arbitrary nonsingular linear transformation of the covariance matrix's first r eigenvectors. They propose a hybrid method that combines local unsupervised updates of matrix A with gradient-based updates of matrix B. The local updates are performed using either Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) or a local symmetric autoencoder loss. The experimental results presented in the paper demonstrate that LoLoRA achieves comparable performance to standard LoRA while significantly reducing memory usage. The authors evaluate LoLoRA on a variety of tasks, including natural language understanding (GLUE benchmark), mathematical reasoning (MetaMathQA and GSM8K), and multimodal fine-tuning (LLaVA). The results show that LoLoRA maintains performance levels close to standard LoRA, while reducing memory usage. The paper also includes ablation studies to analyze the impact of different initialization strategies and local update rules. Overall, the paper presents a promising technique for efficient fine-tuning of LLMs, particularly in resource-constrained environments. The combination of theoretical justification, novel methodology, and empirical validation makes this work a valuable contribution to the field of parameter-efficient fine-tuning. However, as I will discuss in the weaknesses section, there are some limitations to the scope of the experimental evaluation and the depth of the analysis that warrant further investigation.
